answers.rationale: At stage 1 the v2.8 rollout with a JWT library upgrade immediately precedes the symptom; nothing yet discriminates it from the rotation or clock hypotheses.
At stage 2 the v2.7 and v2.8 pods show the same 401 rate.
At stage 1 the rotation is close in time to the symptom, but there is no evidence yet about the gateway's cached key set or which tokens fail.

At stage 2 every sampled rejection is a K2 token, and two dumps presented as production show K1-only key sets last fetched before K2 was published, with a 24-hour refresh. This was the warranted reading then; the later correction does not make it unreasonable at stage 2.
At stage 3 the dumps are shown to be from staging, production agents hold K2, and many K2 tokens are accepted.
At stage 1 a clock-offset alarm exists on some gateway nodes but no rejection-reason or distribution data is available.
At stage 2 there are no 'not yet valid' rejections, offsets are well inside the 30 s leeway, and skewed and unskewed nodes have the same rate.
At stage 2 K2-only rejections are equally consistent with an issuer-side key mismatch; health checks do not test key material, so the alternative is still live even though H2 is supported.
All rejected tokens come from auth-2, whose tokens fail offline verification and whose mounted K2 private key differs from the others.
The mismatch is established, but secret-sync logs for the window are gone and other ways the file could have changed are not excluded.
Equal rates across versions; rejections are fully accounted for by auth-2 tokens.
Rejections map to auth-2 tokens, which fail verification against the published key.
No time-claim rejections; offsets are inside leeway; rates are even across nodes.
Web users are affected too, and sampled rejections are explained by auth-2 key mismatch regardless of client.
Production agents received K2 at 13:31 through the push; staging agents, which are not subscribed, did not.
Failures are confined to K2 tokens from auth-2 and began only after replicas switched to K2 signing; the switch is a necessary condition for the mismatch to matter.
At stage 1 the gateway upgrade is a live candidate; a half-fleet rollback is reversible and discriminates it. Later evidence that v2.8 was not the cause does not make the stage-1 decision wrong.
At stage 2 a stale production key set is the supported mechanism and a forced refresh is low-risk. Judging it by the stage-3 correction is hindsight.
Stops issuance of unverifiable tokens at the source.
Removing K2 from the JWKS would invalidate the valid K2 tokens issued by auth-1 and auth-3 (31% of accepted tokens in the sample), extending the logouts to many more users.
Targets a mechanism already ruled out.
Hardens against the stale-cache failure seen on staging agents, but does not address the auth-2 mechanism causing this incident.

missingInformation: How auth-2 came to hold different K2 key material (secret-sync logs rotated out).
At stages 1-2: which replica issued rejected tokens and whether production key sets contain K2.
hardness.reasoningChain: Rejected tokens are all K2 (E08) -> but many K2 tokens are accepted and production agents hold K2 (E11, E12), so verification capability is not the problem -> rejected tokens all come from auth-2 (E13) -> auth-2's K2 private key does not match the published key (E14) -> signature failures on a third of new tokens after the 14:00 switch (E03, E01).
constructTraps: Marking the stage-2 stale-cache hypothesis refuted or unknown using the stage-3 correction.
Marking the stage-1 rollback or stage-2 refresh as not-recommended because later evidence showed them unnecessary.
Collapsing the issuer-side alternative at stage 2 because the cache hypothesis was supported.
Treating the stage-3 mismatch as proof that secret-sync caused it.
Citing later-stage evidence for stage-scoped items.
